question:
Patient note:
A 71-year-old man was referred from a home-visiting nurse to the ambulatory medical unit late this morning after he complained that his right lower leg had felt “tight and heavy” since yesterday evening and that a few blue surface vessels became conspicuous whenever he let the limb dangle off the edge of the recliner where he has spent most of the past week. Ten days ago he was admitted to a community hospital with influenza A bronchopneumonia complicated by hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring high-flow nasal cannula; although his oxygenation improved, profound fatigue and generalized myalgia led him to remain on bed rest for the final five days of that hospitalization and for three additional days at home after discharge, during which he ambulated only to the bathroom with a walker. He recalls developing an unsteady gait and momentarily over-stretching the posterior calf while pivot-transferring from the commode yesterday, and he believes that minor musculoskeletal strain could easily be responsible for the current discomfort. He denies any blunt trauma, insect bite, laceration, or thermal injury to the extremity and reports no subjective fever, chills, or night sweats since leaving the hospital. Dyspnea is improving, and he has experienced no pleuritic chest pain, cough relapse, palpitations, syncope, flank pain, abdominal cramps, hematuria, or neurologic deficits. A provoked left-popliteal venous thrombosis occurred twelve years ago after spinal fusion surgery and was treated uneventfully with six months of warfarin; follow-up duplex at that time demonstrated complete recanalization, and he has not required long-term anticoagulation. Other medical problems include well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1000 mg twice daily, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine around 1.3 mg/dL, obesity (body mass index 32 kg m⁻²), and chronic systolic heart failure with an ejection fraction of 40 % attributed to prior anterior-wall myocardial infarction; he takes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg every morning, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, and low-dose aspirin. He has never used hormone replacement, glucocorticoids, or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and has no history of malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, nephrotic syndrome, or connective-tissue disorder. He quit smoking fifteen years ago after a 40-pack-year exposure, drinks one beer with dinner on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. On arrival—prior to any analgesic, diuretic adjustment, or antithrombotic therapy—he sat on the examination trolley with the right leg dependent, conversing comfortably without accessory-muscle use. Triage vitals were temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg, heart rate 88 beats min⁻¹ regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 95 % on ambient air. Jugular venous pulsation was 6 cm H₂O at 45°, heart sounds included a soft S3 without murmurs, and bibasilar crackles persisted but were less pronounced than on his discharge documentation. The abdomen was soft and nontender, with no hepatic enlargement or ascites. Inspection of the lower limbs revealed subtle fullness limited to the distal half of the right calf and lateral ankle, whereas the thigh, knee, and foot contours were symmetric. Measuring tape placed exactly 10 cm below the inferior patellar border recorded a circumference of 36.5 cm on the right and 35.4 cm on the left, a difference of 1.1 cm; at 15 cm above the patella the girths were 49.2 cm and 48.9 cm respectively. With the limb dependent for 30 seconds, several straight, non-tortuous superficial veins along the posterolateral calf became engorged and promptly collapsed on elevation. The overlying skin was warm but maintained uniform pink color, and there was no erythema, brawny hyperpigmentation, weeping, bullae, or ulceration. Thumb pressure over the anterior tibial crest rebounded immediately without leaving an indentation. Palpation that traced the expected course of the common femoral vein beneath the inguinal ligament, the superficial femoral tract through the adductor canal, the popliteal fossa, and the posterior tibial groove elicited no discrete tenderness or palpable cord; squeezing the gastrocnemius reproduced only a dull stretch reminiscent of muscle strain. Passive ankle dorsiflexion provoked a gentle pulling sensation but no sharp pain. Hip, knee, and ankle ranges of motion were full and painless; motor strength remained 5/5 throughout, and light-touch sensation was intact. Distal pulses (dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial) were 2 + bilaterally, and capillary refill to all toes was under two seconds. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy, fluctuance, crepitus, or cystic mass was appreciated, and the compartments were soft without tense firmness. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained before blood draw showed normal sinus rhythm at 86 beats min⁻¹ with longstanding Q-waves in V1–V3 but no new ST-T changes. Baseline laboratory studies, drawn prior to any change in medication, revealed hemoglobin 13.1 g dL⁻¹, leukocytes 7.3 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, platelet count 246 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 138 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg dL⁻¹, creatinine 1.36 mg dL⁻¹, AST 22 U L⁻¹, ALT 18 U L⁻¹, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph displayed mild vascular congestion but no focal infiltrate or pleural effusion. Considering the recent prolonged immobility, prior venous event, and the presence of collapsible superficial channels, a repeat deep-vein thrombosis cannot be excluded; nonetheless, chronic venous stasis exacerbated by fluid overload from heart failure—now improving yet still evident—and an uncomplicated gastrocnemius strain appear at least as plausible explanations for the limited, sub-centimeter calf asymmetry in the absence of focal deep-venous tenderness or a sizable circumference difference. Comprehensive duplex ultrasonography from the iliac confluence through the calf veins was therefore ordered while he remained hemodynamically stable, without any immediate anticoagulation, diuretic escalation, or compression therapy administered pending imaging results.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Apply the Wells DVT score before treatment. Each positive DVT criterion adds 1 point; an alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT subtracts 2.
- Bed rest for at least 3 days or recent major surgery: five inpatient days on bed rest qualify → +1.
- Previously documented DVT: prior left popliteal DVT → +1.
- Nonvaricose collateral superficial veins: newly prominent, straight superficial veins on the symptomatic calf → +1.
- Active cancer → 0; paralysis, paresis or recent leg cast → 0.
- Localized tenderness along the deep veins → 0; only muscle stretch discomfort was elicited.
- Entire leg swollen → 0; swelling was confined to the distal calf and ankle.
- Calf circumference difference ≥3 cm → 0; 36.5 − 35.4 = 1.1 cm.
- Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg → 0; pressure left no indentation.
- Alternative diagnosis at least as likely: calf strain or venous stasis with fluid overload → −2.
Sum: 1 + 1 + 1 − 2 = 1.
Final answer: 1
